A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same reward-model evaluation study. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original BoN and PPO experiments, response-distribution and annotation-budget analyses, and overoptimization curves in Tables 1–4 and Figures 3–9.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds model/data variation studies, MT-Bench evaluation, and further sensitivity analyses in its appendices.

M1.justification: The synthetic golden/proxy RM framework, preference-training objective, BoN/PPO optimization, NDR calculation, and response-expansion strategy remain unchanged. Additional model configurations and implementation disclosures do not establish a revision to the proposed procedure.

E1.justification: Appendix 8.4 adds GPT-4o-scored MT-Bench evaluation of downstream policies selected using open-source RMs, extending validation beyond synthetic RewardBench-based regret. MTBench-human already supplied preference-training data in v1; its earlier presence does not constitute this downstream evaluation.

E2.justification: Table 2 retains Mistral-7B, Llama3-8B, Qwen2-7B, and Vicuna-7b. Table 4 retains the same reward-error metrics and Accuracy-pair baseline. The added architecture and downstream-model studies vary experimental configurations rather than introduce competing evaluation methods.

E3.justification: New protocols include Qwen2.5 reward models spanning 0.5–72B parameters, cumulative training-data subsets, Best-of-32 MT-Bench evaluation, a PPO KL-penalty sweep, sample budgets up to 10,000, and a Qwen2.5-7B downstream policy. Figures 6–7 also change the reported response-count sweep from 2–12 to 2–10. These additions do not establish reruns of the retained main experiments.

E4.justification: Appendices 8.3–8.7 add golden/proxy-pair symmetry diagnostics, architecture and training-data sensitivity, KL-penalty sensitivity, larger-sample saturation tests, and validation of response expansion with another downstream model. These substantially extend the robustness questions investigated in v1.

E5.justification: v1 already displays uncertainty bands and ± values. Appendix 8.10 newly specifies 64 test-set samplings, mean/variance reporting for Tables 2–4, and 95% confidence intervals for Figures 5–7; Figure 13 also reports p = 0.001. This documents uncertainty procedures without establishing an increase in training runs or seeds.

E6.justification: Tables 1–4 retain their numerical values, while Figures 4, 6, and 7 revise plotted results. New Figure 12 reports Spearman correlations of 0.8645 for model scaling and 0.458 for training-data subsets; Figure 13 reports 0.635 for RewardBench versus MT-Bench. Further results cover KL sensitivity, sample-size saturation, and another downstream model. These are additional or revised results, not demonstrated same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: v3 adds a KL-constrained normalized definition of policy regret in Equation 2 and explicitly defines the overoptimization ratio, extending its derivation in Appendix 8.9. The Gaussian assumptions and final parametric relationship from v1 remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, RQ3 discussion, and conclusion replace the claim of identifying exogenous variables with the narrower claim that accuracy may fail to capture potential overoptimization. The central claims about imperfect performance prediction and the importance of evaluation-data construction remain.

C2.justification: v3 gives a more specific explanation for why PPO favors evaluation on higher-ranked responses, clarifies diminishing benefits under annotation constraints, and adds interpretations of KL sensitivity and sample-size saturation. These extend the existing interpretation while retaining the central Goodhart-based account and qualifying its causal implications.

D1.justification: Appendix 8.10 and Table 8 newly disclose RM/PPO learning rates, batch sizes, sequence limits, regularization, scheduling, OpenRLHF use, BoN N = 1280, computational scale, and the base-2 KL calculation. Section 2 also clarifies relationships among corrupted training labels. These substantially improve documentation; they do not by themselves establish changes to previously used settings.

R1.justification: v3 adds citations to ChatGLM-RLHF, OpenRLHF, Qwen2.5, RMB, and reward-model robustness for mathematical reasoning, and removes the Voorhees–Tice reference. It also connects the formal regret definition to existing MDP work. The overall positioning within reward evaluation and Goodhart-related research remains stable.

P1.justification: Broad paragraph-level rewriting affects the abstract, introduction's research questions, experimental explanations in Sections 3–5, and conclusion. The expanded appendix places retained metric definitions and theoretical material in Sections 8.8–8.9 instead of 8.3–8.4. The main three-question narrative remains recognizable despite substantial prose revision.

P2.justification: v3 adds Figures 10–15 and Tables 7–8. Existing displays also change: Figure 3 gains fitted lines, uncertainty bands, and correlation annotations; Figure 4 gains explicit rank-bin axis labels; Figures 6–7 change their displayed ranges; and Figure 9 adds accuracy values to its legends. Several retained tables and figures are relocated or reformatted.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v1's narrow synthetic validation and sparse reproducibility reporting through model/data variation studies, MT-Bench evaluation, additional sensitivity tests, and explicit statistical and training details. These strengthen the evidence and make the experiments more auditable. Reporting limitations remain: the open-source RM roster is unspecified, and Table 7's zero-KL Spearman correlation of 0.4840 differs without explanation from Table 1's 0.6102. These limitations constrain particular comparisons but do not outweigh the substantial gains.
